note: Fixed text for each Android check, shown with every finding in the Android report and summary (docs/architecture/android-report.md). The impact levels, high, medium and low as in the project's other tools, are the recorder's default judgement of an issue once confirmed; they are not measured. Each check's sources support its text.

impact.meaning: Can stop the people it affects from completing a task, or make a task very hard for them or likely to fail.
Makes a task harder, slower or more confusing for the people it affects.
An inconvenience; the task can still be done without much extra effort.

5.2.4.name: Only Accessibility-Supported Ways of Using Technologies

checks.title: Touch target smaller than Android's 48 by 48 dp
checks.issue: A control that can be tapped is smaller than 48 by 48 dp, the size Android recommends for anything clickable, touchable or otherwise interactive.
checks.why: Small targets are hard to hit, so people tap the wrong control or have to try several times. Android recommends 48 by 48 dp, about 9 mm, whatever the screen size.
affects: People with hand tremors or limited dexterity
People using the phone with one hand or on the move
People with low vision
checks.basis: Android's guideline and Google's Accessibility Test Framework (ATF). WCAG's own minimum, 24 by 24, is a separate check.
checks.android: Make the control at least 48 by 48 dp. For Views, set android:minWidth and android:minHeight, or enlarge the touchable area with a TouchDelegate without changing the View's size. In Compose, use Modifier.sizeIn(minWidth = 48.dp, minHeight = 48.dp); Material components such as Button and IconButton already do.
checks.flutter: Give the control at least 48 by 48 logical pixels, for example with a SizedBox or ConstrainedBox around it, and keep the theme's materialTapTargetSize at MaterialTapTargetSize.padded so Material controls are padded to 48 by 48.
checks.reactNative: Give the Pressable or Touchable a minWidth and minHeight of 48, or extend its touch area with hitSlop.

checks.title: Touch target smaller than 24 by 24 dp
checks.issue: A control that can be tapped is smaller than 24 by 24 dp, and is not spaced far enough from other targets to be exempt.
checks.why: WCAG 2.5.8 asks for targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or enough space round them; on Android the dp stands for the CSS pixel. Targets this small are easy to miss and easy to confuse with their neighbours.
affects: People with hand tremors or limited dexterity
People who use a knuckle or part of a finger
People using the phone with one hand or on the move
People with low vision
checks.basis: WCAG 2.5.8, applied to Android as WCAG2ICT advises. A target on a line of text, or with an equivalent target of 24 dp and the same name, passes by an exception, judged from the tree; one whose spacing meets only a tappable item it is inside, or one inside it, is a warning, as the two are one target only if they do the same thing.
checks.android: Make the control at least 24 by 24 dp, and preferably Android's 48 by 48 dp. For Views, set android:minWidth and android:minHeight or use a TouchDelegate. In Compose, use Modifier.sizeIn with a minimum width and height.
checks.flutter: Give the control at least 24 by 24 logical pixels, and preferably 48 by 48, with a SizedBox or ConstrainedBox, and keep materialTapTargetSize at MaterialTapTargetSize.padded.
checks.reactNative: Give the control a minWidth and minHeight of at least 24, and preferably 48, or extend its touch area with hitSlop.

checks.title: Touch target smaller than 44 by 44 dp (AAA)
checks.issue: A control that can be tapped is smaller than 44 by 44 dp, the size WCAG 2.5.5 asks for at level AAA.
checks.why: Larger targets are easier for everyone to hit; at AAA, WCAG asks for 44 by 44 CSS pixels, the dp on Android.
affects: People with hand tremors or limited dexterity
People who use a knuckle or part of a finger
People with low vision
People using the phone with one hand or on the move
checks.basis: WCAG 2.5.5, run only at the AAA audit level. A target on a line of text, or with an equivalent target of 44 dp and the same name, passes by an exception, judged from the tree; one inside a tappable item of 44 dp is a warning, as the two are one target only if they do the same thing.
checks.android: Make the control at least 44 by 44 dp, or Android's own 48 by 48 dp, with android:minWidth and android:minHeight, a TouchDelegate, or Compose's Modifier.sizeIn.
checks.flutter: Give the control at least 44 by 44 logical pixels, or 48 by 48, and keep materialTapTargetSize at MaterialTapTargetSize.padded.
checks.reactNative: Give the control a minWidth and minHeight of at least 44, or extend its touch area with hitSlop.

checks.title: Item with nothing for a screen reader to say
checks.issue: An item a screen reader stops at has no text, no content description and no label from another item or its children, so the screen reader has nothing to say for it.
checks.why: Without a name, a screen reader user hears only the item's type, such as "button", or nothing, and cannot tell what it is or what it does.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader such as TalkBack
People with low vision who use a screen reader
People who are deaf-blind and use a braille display
People who use voice control, who need a name to say
checks.basis: ATF SpeakableTextPresentCheck.
checks.android: Give the item a name. For an ImageView, ImageButton or other graphical View, set android:contentDescription; in Compose, set the contentDescription of the Image or Icon. Use android:labelFor when a visible text labels another View. Mark purely decorative images as unimportant for accessibility instead.
checks.flutter: Give the widget a name: set semanticLabel on an Image or Icon, a tooltip on an IconButton, or wrap a custom control in Semantics(label: ...). Wrap a decorative image in ExcludeSemantics instead.
checks.reactNative: Set accessibilityLabel (or aria-label) on the element, and mark it accessible; hide decorative elements with importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants".

checks.title: Same spoken text as other items on the screen
checks.issue: Two or more items on the screen speak the same text, and at least one of them can be tapped, so a screen reader user hears the same words for different items.
checks.why: When items sound alike, a screen reader user cannot tell which one to choose, and may act on the wrong one. Android advises that each description be unique.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader
People who use voice control and say an item's name
People with cognitive disabilities
checks.basis: ATF DuplicateSpeakableTextCheck; it can bear on WCAG 2.4.6 Headings and Labels when the items do different things.
checks.android: Make each label say what is different about its item, for example "Delete entry for 12 May" rather than "Delete". Where several items are one thing, group them into one focusable item.
checks.flutter: Give each Semantics label the detail that tells its item apart, and use MergeSemantics to make a group of widgets one item where they are one thing.
checks.reactNative: Give each element an accessibilityLabel that tells it apart, or group the parts of one thing into one accessible element.

checks.title: Clickable items sharing the same bounds
checks.issue: Two or more clickable items occupy exactly the same area of the screen.
checks.why: A screen reader user may meet the same control twice, or find that one of the two does nothing, and it is unclear which receives a tap.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader
People who use switch access or a keyboard
checks.basis: ATF DuplicateClickableBoundsCheck.
checks.android: Make only one of the overlapping Views or composables clickable, usually the outer one, and remove the click handler from the other. In Compose, clickable on the parent merges its descendants.
checks.flutter: Keep one gesture handler for the area: remove the inner or outer InkWell or GestureDetector, or merge them with MergeSemantics.
checks.reactNative: Keep a single Pressable or Touchable for the area, and make the nested one not accessible.

checks.title: Text field with a content description
checks.issue: An editable text field has a content description, which a screen reader can say instead of the text typed in it.
checks.why: Android's guidance is not to label editable fields with a content description, as it can stop a screen reader from describing, navigating and editing the text entered.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader
People with low vision who use a screen reader
checks.basis: ATF EditableContentDescCheck.
checks.android: Remove the content description from the field. Label it with android:hint, with android:labelFor on a visible label, or with a TextInputLayout; in Compose, use the TextField's label parameter.
checks.flutter: Label the TextField with InputDecoration's labelText or hintText instead of wrapping it in a Semantics label that replaces its value.
checks.reactNative: Label the TextInput with a visible label linked by aria-labelledby, or with placeholder text, rather than an accessibilityLabel that replaces its value.

checks.title: Description that repeats the item's type or state
checks.issue: An item's content description includes words such as "button" or "checked", which the screen reader already says from the item's role and state.
checks.why: The screen reader says the type and state itself, so users hear them twice, for example "Submit button, button"; and a stated state can go out of date.
affects: People who use a screen reader
checks.basis: ATF RedundantDescriptionCheck.
checks.android: Take the type and state words out of the description, for example "Submit", not "Submit button", and give the role with the Role semantics property or the right View class, and the state with stateDescription.
checks.flutter: Take the type and state words out of the Semantics label, and set the matching flags instead, such as button: true or checked.
checks.reactNative: Take the type and state words out of accessibilityLabel, and set accessibilityRole and accessibilityState instead.

checks.title: Item with no role a screen reader recognises
checks.issue: The item's accessibility class name is empty or is not one of Android's own widget classes, so a screen reader cannot say what kind of item it is.
checks.why: Users rely on the role, such as button, switch or edit box, to know what an item does and how to use it.
affects: People who use a screen reader
People who use switch access
checks.basis: ATF ClassNameCheck.
checks.android: Use Android's widgets, or give a custom View the class name of the widget it acts like through its AccessibilityDelegate. In Compose, set the role with Modifier.semantics { role = Role.Button }, or Role.Switch and so on.
checks.flutter: Use Flutter's built-in widgets, or wrap a custom control in Semantics with the flag for its role, such as button: true, textField: true or slider: true.
checks.reactNative: Set accessibilityRole (or role) on custom elements, for example "button" or "adjustable".

checks.title: Reading order links that loop or conflict
checks.issue: Items' "traversal before" and "traversal after" settings form a loop or contradict each other, so the order a screen reader moves in is not defined.
checks.why: A broken order can trap a screen reader user in a loop or skip items, so content is missed or read out of order.
affects: People who use a screen reader
People who use switch access or a keyboard
checks.basis: ATF TraversalOrderCheck.
checks.android: Remove conflicting android:accessibilityTraversalBefore and android:accessibilityTraversalAfter settings, and let the layout order give the reading order where it can. In Compose, use isTraversalGroup and traversalIndex.
checks.flutter: Remove conflicting sortKey values, or give the items OrdinalSortKey values in the order they should be read.
checks.reactNative: Lay the elements out in the order they should be read, rather than reordering them for display.

checks.title: Text contrast below WCAG AA
checks.issue: The text's colour does not differ enough from its background: under 4.5 to 1 for normal text, or under 3 to 1 for large text.
checks.why: Low contrast text is hard or impossible to read for many people, and harder for everyone in bright light.
affects: People with low vision
People with colour vision deficiency
Older people
Anyone in bright light
checks.basis: WCAG 1.4.3, measured on the recorded picture.
checks.android: Choose text and background colours with a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1, or 3 to 1 for text 18sp and over, or 14sp and over in bold. Set them with android:textColor and android:background, or Compose's color parameter and Modifier.background. Watch for colours with transparency, which blend with what is under them.
checks.flutter: Choose theme colours, such as the ColorScheme's onSurface and surface, with a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 between text and background.
checks.reactNative: Choose color and backgroundColor styles with a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1, or 3 to 1 for large text.

checks.title: Text contrast below WCAG AAA
checks.issue: The text's colour does not differ enough from its background for AAA: under 7 to 1 for normal text, or under 4.5 to 1 for large text.
checks.why: Higher contrast makes text readable for more people with low vision, who may not use assistive technology that raises contrast.
affects: People with low vision
People with colour vision deficiency
Older people
checks.basis: WCAG 1.4.6, run only at the AAA audit level.
checks.android: Choose text and background colours with a ratio of at least 7 to 1, or 4.5 to 1 for large text, or offer a high contrast theme.
checks.flutter: Choose theme colours with a ratio of at least 7 to 1, or 4.5 to 1 for large text, or offer a high contrast theme.
checks.reactNative: Choose color and backgroundColor styles with a ratio of at least 7 to 1, or 4.5 to 1 for large text.

checks.title: Control edge or icon contrast below 3 to 1
checks.issue: The parts of a control needed to see it, such as its border, fill or icon, differ from the colours next to them by less than 3 to 1.
checks.why: If people cannot see where a control is, or what state it is in, they may not find or use it.
affects: People with low vision
People with colour vision deficiency
checks.basis: WCAG 1.4.11, measured on the recorded picture. A text field's border, bottom line or background must meet 3 to 1 whatever text it shows, as in figures 31, 32 and 34 of the understanding document. Text read by OCR counts as a control's own only when a word of it is in the control's text from the app; otherwise the finding is a warning, as the picture may not show the control.
checks.android: Give the control's border, fill or icon a colour with at least 3 to 1 contrast against what is next to it, and against the colour of its other states. Thicker strokes help.
checks.flutter: Give the control's border, for example InputDecoration's enabledBorder, its fill or its icon a colour with at least 3 to 1 contrast against its surroundings.
checks.reactNative: Give the control's borderColor, backgroundColor or icon colour at least 3 to 1 contrast against its surroundings.

checks.title: Text field shown only by a bottom line
checks.issue: A text field is shown only by a line along its bottom, with nothing else drawn around it.
checks.why: People who use screen magnification see only part of the screen at a time. Moving down the screen, they can see the field's area without its line, and not know they have found a field they can type in.
affects: People who use screen magnification
People with low vision
checks.basis: Related to WCAG 2.2 conformance requirement 5.2.4, measured on the recorded picture; a warning whatever the line's contrast.
checks.android: Draw a border all the way around the field, such as Material's outlined text field, or give the field a fill with at least 3 to 1 contrast against the colour around it.
checks.flutter: Give the TextField's InputDecoration an OutlineInputBorder in place of the default UnderlineInputBorder, or a fillColor with at least 3 to 1 contrast against its surroundings.
checks.reactNative: Give the TextInput a borderWidth on every side, with a borderColor of at least 3 to 1 contrast, in place of borderBottomWidth alone.

checks.title: Text shown as an image
checks.issue: Words were found inside an image, so the text is a picture rather than real text.
checks.why: Text in an image cannot be resized, recoloured or reflowed to suit the reader, and blurs when enlarged. Unless the image's description gives the same words, a screen reader cannot read it either.
affects: People with low vision who enlarge text or change colours
People with reading or cognitive disabilities who change fonts or spacing
People who use a screen reader, when the image has no matching description
checks.basis: WCAG 1.4.5, from text the PC's OCR read inside an image that no item's text holds, leaving out the screen reader's caption and text past the image's edge. A logotype and an essential presentation are allowed, and text that is part of a picture with significant other visual content is not an image of text; which applies is judged from the picture. Where the app draws its own text, an image whose description holds the words is a warning to check manually.
checks.android: Show the words as real text, in a TextView or Compose Text, styled as needed. Keep images of text only for logos or where the look is essential, and give them a content description with the same words.
checks.flutter: Show the words with a Text widget instead of an Image; for a logo, set the Image's semanticLabel to its words.
checks.reactNative: Show the words with a Text element instead of an Image; for a logo, set accessibilityLabel to its words.

checks.title: Text shown as an image (AAA)
checks.issue: Words were found inside an image; at AAA, only logos and essential images of text are allowed, with no exception for customisable ones.
checks.why: Real text can be adapted to the reader; an image of text cannot.
affects: People with low vision
People with reading or cognitive disabilities
checks.basis: WCAG 1.4.9, run only at the AAA audit level, judged as for 1.4.5; at AAA an image of text that can be customized is not allowed.
checks.android: Show the words as real text; keep images of text only for logos or where the look is essential.
checks.flutter: Show the words with a Text widget; keep images of text only for logos.
checks.reactNative: Show the words with a Text element; keep images of text only for logos.

checks.title: Text shown as a heading but not marked as one
checks.issue: Text is shown as a heading, larger than the text around it or as a short line in capitals, but is not marked as a heading for assistive technology.
checks.why: Screen reader users move by headings to find their way around a screen and to skip to a section. Text that only looks like a heading is read as ordinary text, so the screen's structure is lost to them.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader
People who are deaf-blind and use a braille display
checks.basis: WCAG 1.3.1 as WCAG2ICT applies it to software, and failure F2: a change in the look of text conveys structure without the markup. Found from the recorded picture and the tree: text at least 1.35 times as tall as the screen's body text, or one short line in capitals, that is not marked as a heading and is not inside a control or a field, or a field's label. Whether it is shown as a heading for the content after it is judged from the picture.
checks.android: Mark the text as a heading with android:accessibilityHeading="true" or ViewCompat.setAccessibilityHeading; in Compose, Modifier.semantics { heading() }.
checks.flutter: Wrap the heading's Text in Semantics(header: true).
checks.reactNative: Set accessibilityRole="header" (or role="heading") on the heading's Text.

checks.title: Image with no text alternative
checks.issue: An image that is not a control has no content description, text or label, and no control with a name holds it, so a screen reader says nothing for it. Where the image gives information, that information is lost.
checks.why: Screen reader users hear nothing for the image, so they miss what it shows, such as a status, a chart, a logo that names something or an icon whose meaning the text beside it does not give. A decorative image that is left in the accessibility tree can also be stopped at with nothing said.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader such as TalkBack
People with low vision who use a screen reader
People who are deaf-blind and use a braille display
checks.basis: WCAG 1.1.1, from the tree and the recorded picture: a visible image with no content description, text or label, that is not a control and that no control with a name holds; an image mostly under controls with a name, or under 2 dp on its shorter side, is left out. A warning for a person to confirm whether it gives information unless the project's model for vision-based checks was asked; its answer is the model's inference and says so.
checks.android: Give an image that gives information a content description that says what it shows, with android:contentDescription or setContentDescription; in Compose, set the contentDescription of the Image or Icon. Mark a decorative image as not important for accessibility with android:importantForAccessibility="no", or in Compose give it contentDescription = null.
checks.flutter: Give an image that gives information a semanticLabel, or wrap it in Semantics(label: ...). Wrap a decorative image in ExcludeSemantics, or set excludeFromSemantics: true on the Image.
checks.reactNative: Give an image that gives information an accessibilityLabel (or alt), and mark it accessible. Hide a decorative image with accessible={false} and importantForAccessibility="no".

checks.title: Icon that contradicts its control's name
checks.issue: A control shown as an icon has a name that says one thing while its icon is the usual symbol for something else, such as a bin icon on a control named "Save".
checks.why: A person who sees the icon and a person who hears the name expect different things. Screen reader users who can see some of the screen, and people who use voice control by saying what a control is called, are misled, and either the name or the icon gives the wrong idea of what the control does.
affects: People who use a screen reader and can see some of the screen
People who use voice control, such as Voice Access
People with cognitive disabilities
People who are blind and use a screen reader, where the name is the one that is wrong
checks.basis: WCAG 1.1.1, from the tree and the recorded picture: an image that is a control, with a description or text of its own as its name, judged against the picture only by the project's model for vision-based checks, which first says whether the image is an icon at all. Every finding is a warning, the model's inference, for a person to verify; with no model there is no finding.
checks.android: Make the content description say what the control does, and use the icon commonly used for that action; in Compose, set the contentDescription of the Icon or IconButton to match it. Where the icon is right, correct the name; where the name is right, change the icon.
checks.flutter: Make the IconButton's tooltip or the Semantics label say what the control does, and use the icon commonly used for that action.
checks.reactNative: Make the accessibilityLabel say what the control does, and use the icon commonly used for that action.

checks.title: Description that does not match its image
checks.issue: An image that is not a control has a content description or text that names or describes something the image does not show, or contradicts it.
checks.why: Screen reader users are given the description in place of the image, so a description that does not match gives them the wrong information, and people who can see some of the screen hear something other than what is shown.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader such as TalkBack
People with low vision who use a screen reader
People who are deaf-blind and use a braille display
checks.basis: WCAG 1.1.1, from the tree and the recorded picture: an image that is not a control, with a description or text of its own, judged against the picture only by the project's model for vision-based checks. Every finding is a warning, the model's inference, for a person to verify; with no model there is no finding.
checks.android: Give the image a content description that says what it shows or stands for, with android:contentDescription or setContentDescription; in Compose, set the contentDescription of the Image. Where the image only decorates, mark it as not important for accessibility, or in Compose give it contentDescription = null.
checks.flutter: Give the image a semanticLabel, or wrap it in Semantics(label: ...), that says what it shows or stands for; wrap a decorative image in ExcludeSemantics.
checks.reactNative: Give the image an accessibilityLabel (or alt) that says what it shows or stands for; hide a decorative image with accessible={false} and importantForAccessibility="no".

checks.title: Visible label not in the spoken name
checks.issue: The words shown on a control are not part of the name a screen reader or voice control uses for it.
checks.why: People who use voice control say what they see, such as "Tap Send"; if the name is different, the command does not work. Screen reader users who can see also hear a name that does not match the screen.
affects: People who use voice control, such as Voice Access
People who use a screen reader and can see some of the screen
People with cognitive disabilities
checks.basis: WCAG 2.5.3.
checks.android: Make the content description, or the Compose contentDescription, include the visible words, ideally at the start. Often the fix is to remove a content description that replaces visible text.
checks.flutter: Make the Semantics label include the visible text, ideally at the start, or remove a label that replaces the Text widget's own text.
checks.reactNative: Make accessibilityLabel include the visible text, ideally at the start, or remove it so the text is used.

checks.title: Visible label not at the start of the spoken name
checks.issue: The words shown on a control are in its spoken name, but not at the start.
checks.why: WCAG advises that the visible text start the name, as voice control users say the visible words and screen reader users hear the start first.
affects: People who use voice control
People who use a screen reader and can see some of the screen
checks.basis: Best practice from the understanding document for WCAG 2.5.3.
checks.android: Put the visible words first in the content description, and any extra detail after them.
checks.flutter: Put the visible words first in the Semantics label.
checks.reactNative: Put the visible words first in accessibilityLabel.

checks.title: Clickable item that the keyboard may not reach
checks.issue: An item can be clicked but is not marked focusable, so a keyboard or switch user may not be able to move to it and use it.
checks.why: Everything that can be done by touch must also be possible by keyboard. Whether the keyboard really reaches the item is to be confirmed by a person, as the tree alone cannot show it.
affects: People who use a keyboard or switch access
People who cannot use a touch screen
Some people with hand tremors
People who are blind and use a keyboard with a screen reader
checks.basis: WCAG 2.1.1; a warning for a person to confirm with a keyboard.
checks.android: Make the item focusable, android:focusable="true" or View.setFocusable, or use a widget that is, such as Button. In Compose, clickable items are focusable; make sure custom gesture handlers also respond to the keyboard.
checks.flutter: Use a widget that takes keyboard focus, such as InkWell or a Material button, or wrap a custom control in FocusableActionDetector, rather than a bare GestureDetector.
checks.reactNative: Use Pressable or a Touchable, and set focusable on Android where a View handles touches itself.

checks.title: Text field with no label
checks.issue: A text field has no label: no visible text linked to it and no hint, so people are not told what to enter.
checks.why: Without a label, people may not know what the field is for, especially once a placeholder is gone, and screen readers have nothing to say.
affects: People with cognitive, language or learning disabilities
People who use a screen reader
Everyone, when the field's purpose is not obvious
checks.basis: WCAG 3.3.2.
checks.android: Give the field a visible label linked with android:labelFor, a hint with android:hint, or use a TextInputLayout. In Compose, use the TextField's label parameter.
checks.flutter: Set InputDecoration's labelText, and a hintText where an example helps.
checks.reactNative: Show a visible label next to the TextInput and link it with aria-labelledby, or give it a placeholder and accessibilityLabel.

checks.title: Text field with no accessible name
checks.issue: A text field has no name a screen reader can say: no label, hint or linked text.
checks.why: A screen reader user hears only "edit box" and cannot tell what to type.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader
People who use voice control
checks.basis: WCAG 4.1.2.
checks.android: Name the field with android:hint, with android:labelFor on its visible label, or with a TextInputLayout; in Compose, use the TextField's label parameter. Do not use a content description on the field.
checks.flutter: Set InputDecoration's labelText, or hintText, on the TextField.
checks.reactNative: Give the TextInput an accessibilityLabel, or link a visible label with aria-labelledby.

checks.title: Field marked invalid with no error message
checks.issue: An item is marked invalid but has no error text that says what is wrong.
checks.why: People need to know that there is an error and what it is to correct it; a screen reader says the error text when it is set on the field.
affects: People who are blind or have low vision
People with cognitive, language or learning disabilities
checks.basis: WCAG 3.3.1.
checks.android: Set the error text on the field, for example with TextInputLayout.setError, so that it is both shown and given to accessibility services. In Compose, set the error semantics property with the message.
checks.flutter: Set InputDecoration's errorText to a message saying what is wrong and how to fix it.
checks.reactNative: Show the error as text next to the field and include it in the field's accessibilityHint or label, and announce it when it appears.

checks.title: Expandable item with no expanded state
checks.issue: An item can be expanded or collapsed, but does not say which it is.
checks.why: A screen reader user cannot tell whether more content has opened, or whether to act on the item again.
affects: People who use a screen reader
checks.basis: WCAG 4.1.2.
checks.android: Expose the expand and collapse actions and the state, for example by setting the expanded state on the item's AccessibilityNodeInfo in its AccessibilityDelegate. In Compose, use the expand and collapse semantics actions, or a stateDescription.
checks.flutter: Set Semantics(expanded: true or false) on a custom expanding widget.
checks.reactNative: Set accessibilityState={{ expanded: true }} or false on the element.

checks.title: Slider with no range or value
checks.issue: A slider or other adjustable item does not give its current value and range to accessibility services.
checks.why: A screen reader user cannot tell the value or how far it can go, and may not be able to change it.
affects: People who use a screen reader
checks.basis: WCAG 4.1.2.
checks.android: Use a SeekBar or Compose Slider, or give a custom slider RangeInfo through its AccessibilityDelegate. In Compose, set progressBarRangeInfo.
checks.flutter: Use the Slider widget, or wrap a custom one in Semantics(slider: true, value: ..., increasedValue: ..., decreasedValue: ...) with onIncrease and onDecrease.
checks.reactNative: Set accessibilityRole="adjustable" and accessibilityValue={{ min, max, now }}.

checks.title: Screen with no title
checks.issue: The screen has no title that a screen reader can announce: its window title and pane titles are missing or blank.
checks.why: A title tells people where they are when a screen opens; without it, screen reader users must explore to find out.
affects: People who use a screen reader
People with cognitive disabilities or limited short-term memory
checks.basis: WCAG 2.4.2 as WCAG2ICT applies it to software.
checks.android: Give each screen a title: the activity's title (android:label or setTitle), or a pane title with android:accessibilityPaneTitle or View.setAccessibilityPaneTitle; in Compose, Modifier.semantics { paneTitle = ... }.
checks.flutter: Give each route a name: wrap the screen's title in Semantics(namesRoute: true) inside the route. On Android 9 and later, Flutter sets the route's name as the pane title, and a single space when nothing names the route.
checks.reactNative: Set a title for each screen in the navigator, and announce it when the screen opens.

checks.title: Screen title shared with other screens
checks.issue: The screen's title is the same as another screen's in the same app.
checks.why: When different screens share a title, people cannot tell from it which screen they are on.
affects: People who use a screen reader
People with cognitive disabilities or limited short-term memory
checks.basis: WCAG 2.4.2 as WCAG2ICT applies it to software.
checks.android: Give each screen a title of its own, describing its purpose, with the activity's title or a pane title.
checks.flutter: Give each route its own name with Semantics(namesRoute: true) on the screen's title, rather than the app's name on every screen.
checks.reactNative: Give each screen its own title in the navigator.

checks.title: Screen with no heading
checks.issue: No item shown on the screen is marked as a heading.
checks.why: Screen reader users move by headings to find their way around a screen; with none marked, they must go item by item.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader
People who are deaf-blind and use a braille display
checks.basis: WCAG 1.3.1 as WCAG2ICT applies it to software.
checks.android: Mark the screen's title and section titles as headings with android:accessibilityHeading="true" or ViewCompat.setAccessibilityHeading; in Compose, Modifier.semantics { heading() }.
checks.flutter: Wrap each heading's Text in Semantics(header: true).
checks.reactNative: Set accessibilityRole="header" (or role="heading") on each heading's Text.

checks.title: First heading far from the top of the screen
checks.issue: The topmost heading starts below the top quarter of the screen, so the screen's title may not be marked as a heading.
checks.why: People who move by headings expect the first one to name the screen; if it is lower, they may miss what comes before it.
affects: People who use a screen reader
checks.basis: The recorder's own warning for a person to review; not a WCAG requirement.
checks.android: If the screen has a title near the top, mark it as a heading as well.
checks.flutter: If the screen has a title near the top, wrap it in Semantics(header: true) as well.
checks.reactNative: If the screen has a title near the top, set accessibilityRole="header" on it as well.

checks.title: Many items marked as headings
checks.issue: More than half of the items a screen reader stops at are marked as headings.
checks.why: When most items are headings, moving by heading is no quicker than moving item by item, and headings no longer show the screen's structure.
affects: People who use a screen reader
checks.basis: The recorder's own warning for a person to review; not a WCAG requirement.
checks.android: Mark only the screen's title and the titles of its sections as headings.
checks.flutter: Use Semantics(header: true) only on real section titles.
checks.reactNative: Use accessibilityRole="header" only on real section titles.

checks.title: Status message not announced
checks.issue: A message appeared by itself and went within 5 seconds, with no touch between, but it was not in a live region, not announced and not in a titled pane, so a screen reader is not told of it.
checks.why: People who cannot see the message miss confirmations, errors and progress, such as "Saved" or "Loading".
affects: People who are blind or have low vision
People with some cognitive disabilities
checks.basis: WCAG 4.1.3.
checks.android: Put status text in a live region, android:accessibilityLiveRegion="polite" or View.setAccessibilityLiveRegion; in Compose, Modifier.semantics { liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite }. View.announceForAccessibility is deprecated from Android 16, API level 36.
checks.flutter: Wrap the message in Semantics(liveRegion: true), or call SemanticsService.announce with it.
checks.reactNative: Set accessibilityLiveRegion="polite" on the message's element, or call AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility.

checks.title: No live region anywhere in the app
checks.issue: In the whole recording, no item of the app was in a live region, and the app made no announcement and showed no toast.
checks.why: Apps usually have status messages, such as saved, sent or loading; if none is exposed, screen reader users are likely to miss them.
affects: People who are blind or have low vision
People with some cognitive disabilities
checks.basis: WCAG 4.1.3; a warning for a person to confirm that the app has status messages.
checks.android: Find the app's status messages and put each in a live region, android:accessibilityLiveRegion="polite", or Compose's liveRegion semantics.
checks.flutter: Find the app's status messages and wrap each in Semantics(liveRegion: true).
checks.reactNative: Find the app's status messages and set accessibilityLiveRegion="polite" on each.

checks.title: Text gone by itself before the time chosen
checks.issue: Text went away by itself, with no touch, sooner than the time looked for: 5 seconds, or the phone's Time to take action setting when one was chosen.
checks.why: People who read slowly, or who need time to find and act on a message, lose it before they are done. Android lets users choose a longer Time to take action, which apps can read.
affects: People who read slowly or have reading disabilities
People who use a screen reader
People with low vision who use magnification
People with cognitive or motor disabilities
checks.basis: WCAG 2.2.1.
checks.android: Keep messages up until the user dismisses them, or for the user's chosen time from AccessibilityManager.getRecommendedTimeoutMillis.
checks.flutter: Show messages until dismissed, for example a SnackBar with an action and a long duration, or read the Android timeout through a platform channel.
checks.reactNative: Keep messages up until dismissed, or use AccessibilityInfo.getRecommendedTimeoutMillis for the time to show them.

checks.title: Text gone as new content appeared
checks.issue: Text went away by itself as new content appeared, as when loading finishes; the recording cannot show whether it was on a timer.
checks.why: If the text was on a timer, people may lose it before they can read it; if it was a loading message, people should be told when loading finishes.
affects: People who read slowly or have reading disabilities
People who use a screen reader
People with cognitive disabilities
checks.basis: WCAG 2.2.1; a warning for a person to confirm.
checks.android: If the text is on a timer, keep it up until dismissed or for the user's chosen time. If it is a loading message, make the change known, for example with a live region or a pane title on the new content.
checks.flutter: If the text is on a timer, show it until dismissed. If it is a loading message, announce the result with Semantics(liveRegion: true) or SemanticsService.announce.
checks.reactNative: If the text is on a timer, show it until dismissed. If it is a loading message, announce the result with a live region or AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility.

checks.title: Text updating by itself
checks.issue: An item's text changed in place twice or more with no touch, as auto-updating content does.
checks.why: Content that updates by itself can distract people from the rest of the screen, and a screen reader may keep reading it out; WCAG asks for a way to pause, stop or hide it, unless it is essential.
affects: People with attention or cognitive disabilities
People with reading disabilities
People who use a screen reader
checks.basis: WCAG 2.2.2; a warning for a person to confirm.
checks.android: Give a way to pause, stop or hide the updates, or to set how often they come. Do not put frequently updating content, such as a countdown, in a live region.
checks.flutter: Give a way to pause or hide the updating widget, and do not wrap frequently updating text in Semantics(liveRegion: true).
checks.reactNative: Give a way to pause or hide the updates, and do not put frequently updating text in a live region.

checks.title: Content moving by itself
checks.issue: The phone's picture kept changing for more than 5 seconds with no touch, as an animation, carousel or video does; this was found from the video and is approximate.
checks.why: Movement that lasts more than 5 seconds and cannot be paused distracts people from the rest of the screen and can make it hard to read.
affects: People with attention or cognitive disabilities
People with reading disabilities
People with vestibular disorders
checks.basis: WCAG 2.2.2; a warning from the video, for a person to confirm.
checks.android: Give a pause or stop control for movement that lasts more than 5 seconds, and respect the system's Remove animations setting.
checks.flutter: Give a pause or stop control, and stop or shorten animations when MediaQuery's disableAnimations is set.
checks.reactNative: Give a pause or stop control, and stop animations when AccessibilityInfo reports that reduce motion is on.

checks.title: Change of context when an item got the focus
checks.issue: Moving the focus to an item, with nothing activated, was followed within 1.5 seconds by a change of context, such as a new window or dialog.
checks.why: People expect moving to an item to be safe; if the screen changes, they lose their place and may not know what happened.
affects: People who use a keyboard or switch access
People who use a screen reader
People with cognitive disabilities
checks.basis: WCAG 3.2.1.
checks.android: Open windows, dialogs and new screens only when the user activates something, not in a focus listener such as View.OnFocusChangeListener or Compose's onFocusChanged.
checks.flutter: Do not navigate or open dialogs from a FocusNode listener or onFocusChange; do it when the user activates a control.
checks.reactNative: Do not navigate or open dialogs from onFocus; do it from onPress.

checks.title: Change of context when TalkBack's focus moved
checks.issue: TalkBack's focus moving to an item, with no double tap, touch or key, was followed within 1.5 seconds by a change of context.
checks.why: Screen reader users explore a screen by moving TalkBack's focus; if that alone changes the screen, they cannot explore safely.
affects: People who are blind and use a screen reader
People with low vision who use a screen reader
checks.basis: WCAG 3.2.1.
checks.android: Do not act on accessibility focus events, such as TYPE_VIEW_ACCESSIBILITY_FOCUSED; act only when the user activates the item.
checks.flutter: Do not navigate or open dialogs from Semantics' onDidGainAccessibilityFocus; act only on the item's activation.
checks.reactNative: Do not navigate or open dialogs on accessibility focus; act only from onPress or the activate action.

checks.title: Change of context when a setting was changed
checks.issue: Changing a control's setting, such as a switch or choice, was followed within 1.5 seconds by a change of context, with no further touch or key.
checks.why: People do not expect changing a setting to move them somewhere else, unless they were told beforehand.
affects: People who are blind or have low vision
People with cognitive, reading or intellectual disabilities
checks.basis: WCAG 3.2.2; a warning, as it is allowed when the user was told of it before using the control.
checks.android: Let the user change settings first and then confirm with a button, or say next to the control what will happen when it changes.
checks.flutter: Avoid navigating from onChanged; add a confirm button, or say beforehand what will happen.
checks.reactNative: Avoid navigating from onValueChange or onChange; add a confirm button, or say beforehand what will happen.

checks.title: Screen did not turn with the phone
checks.issue: The phone was held turned, with Auto-rotate on, for the time chosen, and the screen stayed in the other orientation, as when an app restricts its display to one orientation.
checks.why: People who have their phone mounted in one position, such as on a wheelchair, or who need a wider screen to read, cannot use an app locked to the other orientation.
affects: People with a mounted phone, such as on a wheelchair
People with low vision who use landscape for larger text
checks.basis: WCAG 1.3.4; a warning, as one orientation is allowed where it is essential.
checks.android: Remove android:screenOrientation from the activity in the manifest, or set it to a value that follows the sensor, unless one orientation is essential.
checks.flutter: Do not restrict SystemChrome.setPreferredOrientations to one orientation, unless it is essential.
checks.reactNative: Do not lock the orientation in the app's AndroidManifest or orientation settings, unless it is essential.

checks.title: Letters spaced apart with spaces
checks.issue: The item's text spaces the letters of a word with space characters, such as "W e l c o m e".
checks.why: A screen reader may read the letters one at a time instead of the word.
affects: People who use a screen reader
People who are deaf-blind and use a braille display
checks.basis: WCAG 1.3.2, failure F32.
checks.android: Write the word normally and space the letters with android:letterSpacing, or Compose's letterSpacing in the TextStyle.
checks.flutter: Write the word normally and space the letters with TextStyle(letterSpacing: ...).
checks.reactNative: Write the word normally and space the letters with the letterSpacing style.

checks.title: Columns made with spaces
checks.issue: Two or more lines of the item's text use runs of spaces or tabs to line words up in columns.
checks.why: A screen reader reads across the columns line by line, so the values lose their headings and the meaning is lost.
affects: People who use a screen reader
People who are deaf-blind and use a braille display
People who enlarge text, as the columns break
checks.basis: WCAG 1.3.2, failure F33.
checks.android: Lay the columns out with layout, such as a TableLayout, GridLayout or Compose Row and Column, with one item for each cell.
checks.flutter: Lay the columns out with a Table, Row or GridView, with one Text for each cell.
checks.reactNative: Lay the columns out with Views in rows, with one Text for each cell.

checks.title: Line break in mid-sentence
checks.issue: The item's text has a line break in the middle of a sentence, where the line before does not end a sentence and the next starts with a lowercase letter.
checks.why: A hard line break can make a screen reader pause or split the sentence, and the text cannot reflow when it is enlarged.
affects: People who use a screen reader
People who enlarge text
checks.basis: WCAG 1.3.2.
checks.android: Take the line break out of the text and let the TextView or Text wrap it.
checks.flutter: Take the line break out of the string and let the Text widget wrap it.
checks.reactNative: Take the line break out of the string and let the Text element wrap it.
